name: Infected Tree
description: Byteland is a beautiful land known because of its beautiful trees. Misha has found a binary tree with $$$n$$$ vertices, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. A binary tree is an acyclic connected bidirectional graph containing $$$n$$$ vertices and $$$n - 1$$$ edges. Each vertex has a degree at most $$$3$$$, whereas the root is the vertex with the number $$$1$$$ and it has a degree at most $$$2$$$. Unfortunately, the root got infected. The following process happens $$$n$$$ times: Misha either chooses a non-infected (and not deleted) vertex and deletes it with all edges which have an end in this vertex or just does nothing. Then, the infection spreads to each vertex that is connected by an edge to an already infected vertex (all already infected vertices remain infected). As Misha does not have much time to think, please tell him what is the maximum number of vertices he can save from the infection (note that deleted vertices are not counted as saved).
input_specification: There are several test cases in the input data. The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1\leq t\leq 5000$$$) — the number of test cases. This is followed by the test cases description. The first line of each test case contains one integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2\leq n\leq 3\cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of vertices of the tree. The $$$i$$$-th of the following $$$n-1$$$ lines in the test case contains two positive integers $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq u_i, v_i \leq n$$$), meaning that there exists an edge between them in the graph. It is guaranteed that the graph is a binary tree rooted at $$$1$$$. It is also guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases won't exceed $$$3\cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output the maximum number of vertices Misha can save.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1689C — Infected Tree [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
